title: Language models lack systematicity in generating and updating hypotheses
claim: One ambiguous set of examples can be probed three ways, by prediction, evaluation, and generation, to measure the same underlying posterior.
layout: Single panel, three color-coded rows, prompt left and LLM output right
description: A single rounded panel shows a chat-style prompt schematic. At the top, a System message explains that a program says yes or no to numbers from 1 to 100 depending on a simple concept. Below it, the User message says the program says yes to 16, 8, 2, 64. Under that are three horizontal rows, color-coded green, blue and orange. Each row has a prompt box on the left and a matching LLM assistant output box on the right. Green, Posterior predict, asks whether the program would say yes to a number y, and the output is Yes/No. Blue, Hypothesis evaluation, gives a numbered candidate list such as powers of 2 and even numbers, and the output is a JSON dictionary of probabilities. Orange, Hypothesis generation, asks for 10 candidate concepts, and the output is a JSON list of hypotheses with confidences. The eye goes first to the colored row titles.
caption: Three measurements of the posterior over hypotheses in the number game. The schematic shows how we prompt LLMs to measure their posterior over hypotheses. Posterior prediction queries the LLM with one integer in the integer domain at a time and records the model-generated probability that the integer belongs to the same concept as the current examples, yielding a membership probability for every integer in the domain. Hypothesis evaluation shows the candidate hypothesis list, the rule hypotheses and a few interval hypotheses around the current examples drawn from the hypothesis space of the Bayesian model, and records the LLM's confidence in each listed hypothesis. Hypothesis generation asks the LLM to generate 10 different hypotheses and associated confidences given the examples.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex problems, from automated code debugging to science itself. Such problems require generating plausible hypotheses from sparse, noisy, and ambiguous data and updating them as more information arrives. Yet how closely LLMs approach optimal inductive reasoning remains unclear. We study this question in the classic number game, in which a learner infers a concept from a few ambiguous positive integers: $\{2, 16, 4, 8\}$, for example, is explained both by ``powers of 2'' and by ``numbers up to 20.'' We probe the concepts LLMs hypothesize from the observed examples and use their behavioral patterns to understand how they generate and update hypotheses. We measure the LLM posterior over hypotheses in three tasks (prediction, evaluation, and generation) and compare LLM behavior with a Bayesian model and with humans. LLMs favor narrower hypotheses than humans and show a robust evaluation--generation gap: in evaluation they select hypotheses more consistent with the observed examples, whereas in generation they propose narrower hypotheses that are more often rules. They also update poorly: as examples accumulate, their accuracy declines while their confidence grows. Thinking reduces, and can even reverse, the gap; it also broadens the hypotheses LLMs favor, raising accuracy while lowering confidence. Whereas prior studies have shown that LLMs are good hypothesis proposers, our results and further comparisons with the Bayesian model show that LLM inductive reasoning lacks coherence across the three tasks, suggesting that LLMs do not maintain a stable representation shared across tasks that make the same demand. Our results highlight a limitation of LLMs in inductive inference, particularly in settings such as science, where hypotheses must go beyond the data.
